notes.b: Food has to supply energy and raw materials for growth and repair. A balanced diet does this without leaving the body short of anything or overloaded with anything.
points: A balanced diet contains all the nutrients (carbohydrate, protein, lipid, vitamins and minerals), together with water and dietary fibre, in the right amounts and proportions to meet a person's needs, with enough energy but not too much.
Balanced means right proportions, not equal amounts from each food group. A person needs far more starchy food and vegetables than fats, for example.

Malnutrition is any diet that does not meet the body's needs. Undernutrition is too little energy or too little of a nutrient, e.g. iron-deficiency anaemia or rickets (a bone disease caused by too little vitamin D).
Overnutrition is too much energy or too much of a nutrient, e.g. obesity (a body mass well above the healthy range, from long-term excess energy) or too much salt.
Energy balance: if the energy taken in from food equals the energy used in metabolism (the body's chemical reactions) and activity, body mass stays the same.

Excess energy is stored as fat, causing weight gain. Too little energy means the body uses its glycogen (the short-term carbohydrate store), then fat, and eventually muscle protein, so weight is lost.
notes.tip: If asked what a balanced diet is, mention nutrients, water, fibre, the right proportions and the right amount of energy. Do not say equal amounts of each food group.

notes.b: The Food Pyramid turns the idea of a balanced diet into a picture of how much of each food group to eat. The wider the shelf, the more servings you should have from it.
points: Ireland's Food Pyramid (Department of Health, 2016) is a guide to a balanced diet, in which most servings come from the lower shelves.
The lower shelves are vegetables, salad and fruit (5 to 7 servings a day), and wholemeal cereals, breads, potatoes, pasta and rice.

Milk, yoghurt and cheese (3 servings a day, or 5 for ages 9 to 18, because teenagers are growing fast and need more calcium) and meat, poultry, fish, eggs, beans and nuts (2 servings) are in the middle.
Fats, spreads and oils are for very small amounts, and the top shelf, foods and drinks high in fat, sugar and salt, is not for every day.
notes.tip: Learn the servings for each shelf exactly as given here, including the 5 dairy servings for ages 9 to 18, and do not add serving figures of your own.

notes.b: Body mass index (BMI) gives a quick number for whether a person's mass is suitable for their height. It is a screening tool and you may be asked to calculate and interpret it.
points: Body mass index (BMI) is mass in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres.
For adults, the World Health Organization classes 18.5 to 24.9 as a healthy weight, 25 to 29.9 as overweight and 30 or more as obese; below 18.5 is underweight.
BMI does not distinguish fat from muscle, so a muscular athlete can have a high BMI even with little body fat. It also does not show where fat is stored.
Children and teenagers are still growing, so they are assessed with growth charts for their age and sex instead of the adult categories.
Worked example: 70 kg ÷ (1.75 m × 1.75 m) = 70 ÷ 3.06 = 22.9, a healthy weight.
notes.tip: Show the squaring of height in your working, then place the answer in the correct WHO category. If asked for a limitation, say BMI cannot tell fat from muscle or show where fat is stored.

notes.b: A balanced diet is not the same for everyone. What a person needs depends on their health, their age, their gender and how active they are, and each factor has a biological reason.
points: Health: illnesses change needs. People with coeliac disease (an immune reaction to gluten, a protein in wheat) must avoid gluten, and people with type 1 diabetes match carbohydrate intake to their insulin. There is more on coeliac disease in Emerging diseases and society.

People with high blood pressure are advised to eat less salt, and people with anaemia need more iron to make haemoglobin; people recovering from injury or surgery need more protein for repair, and people with lactose intolerance avoid or limit lactose (milk sugar) and need other calcium sources.

Age, children and teenagers: growing children need more protein, calcium and vitamin D for bones, and more energy per kilogram of body mass than adults. Babies' needs are met by breast milk or formula.
The teenage growth spurt raises energy, protein, calcium and iron needs, which is why the Food Pyramid gives 5 dairy servings for ages 9 to 18.

Age, older people: metabolic rate and activity usually fall, so less energy is needed. Protein (to limit muscle loss), calcium and vitamin D (to limit bone loss and osteoporosis, brittle bones), fibre (constipation is more common) and water (the sense of thirst weakens with age) remain important.

Gender: on average males have more muscle and a larger body, so they need more energy and protein. Females who menstruate lose iron in blood each month, so they need more iron. Pregnancy and breastfeeding raise the need for energy, protein, calcium and iron.
Folic acid (a B vitamin) is advised before and in early pregnancy, and pregnant women should avoid alcohol and liver, which is high in vitamin A.

Activity: active people use more energy, so they need more starchy carbohydrate (builds glycogen stores), protein for muscle repair, and water and salt to replace sweat; inactive (sedentary) people use less energy, so they need less, and eating as though active leads to weight gain.
notes.tip: Questions ask you to explain why the needs of a teenager, an older person, a pregnant woman or an athlete differ. Name the nutrient and give the biological reason, such as growth, bone loss, iron lost in blood or energy used.

notes.b: Eating from every food group is not enough on its own. Eating a range of different foods is what makes sure nothing is missed.
points: No single food contains every nutrient in the right proportions, so a varied diet from all the food groups is the most reliable way to get all the vitamins, minerals, essential amino acids and essential fatty acids (the ones the body cannot make for itself).

Variety within groups also matters because different fruits and vegetables supply different vitamins, minerals and fibre types, e.g. citrus fruit for vitamin C, green leafy vegetables for iron, calcium and vitamin K, and carrots for beta-carotene.

Combining plant proteins, e.g. beans with cereal, supplies all the essential amino acids, because each food makes up for what the other lacks. There is more on this in Metabolic roles and nutritional sources.
notes.tip: Do not write that vegetarians or vegans cannot get enough protein. Combined plant proteins supply all the essential amino acids.

notes.b: Water makes up most of the body and is constantly being lost, so a diet is only balanced if it also replaces water.
points: Water is lost every day in urine, sweat, breath and faeces, and must be replaced from drinks and food. Needs rise in hot weather, during exercise, with fever, vomiting or diarrhoea, and when breastfeeding. There is more on the roles of water in Water.

Signs of dehydration (too little water in the body) are thirst, dark-yellow urine in small volumes, headache, tiredness and poor concentration. The urine is dark and scant because the hormone ADH makes the kidneys hold on to water at Higher Level.
Severe dehydration is dangerous, especially in babies and older people.
Water is the best drink. Sugar-sweetened drinks supply water but also free sugars (sugars added to foods and drinks, explained under high-sugar diets below).
notes.tip: Link each sign of dehydration to the body's water shortage. Do not give a daily litre figure.

notes.b: Fibre is the part of plant food that passes through you without being digested, yet it is essential for a healthy gut. It supplies almost no energy and is not absorbed.
points: Dietary fibre, or roughage, is plant material that human enzymes cannot digest, mainly cellulose from plant cell walls. There is more on cellulose in Structures of biomolecules.

Sources of fibre are wholegrain cereals and wholemeal bread, brown rice, vegetables, fruit (especially with skins), beans, peas and lentils, and nuts and seeds. There is no fibre in meat, fish, eggs or dairy produce.

Fibre adds bulk and absorbs water, so faeces are soft and large. This gives the gut muscles something to push against, keeps peristalsis (the waves of muscle contraction that move food along the gut) effective and prevents constipation.
Fibre makes food more filling and slows the absorption of sugar, which helps control body mass and blood glucose.
High-fibre diets are linked to a lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and bowel cancer.
Bacteria in the colon ferment some fibre, which supports a healthy gut microbiome (the community of microorganisms living in the gut).
Raising fibre intake suddenly can cause wind and bloating, and fibre needs extra water to work. Very large amounts of bran can reduce the absorption of some minerals such as iron and calcium.
notes.tip: For the importance of fibre, link bulk and water to peristalsis and constipation. Do not call fibre a nutrient that is absorbed, and do not say it cleans the gut.

notes.h: How to research a dietary claim (Skills)
notes.b: Newspapers and adverts make many claims about food. Researching a claim in steps lets you judge whether the evidence is reliable before you accept it.
points: 1. Pose a specific, testable question, e.g. 'Does a vegan diet supply enough iron for teenage girls?'

2. Find several reliable sources, such as public health bodies, peer-reviewed reviews (checked by other scientists before publication) and textbooks. There is more on this in Recognising bias and evaluating sources.
3. Check who funded and wrote each source, and whether it sells a product, because money can bias what is reported.

4. Judge the type of evidence. Most diet evidence comes from observational studies of large populations, which show links (correlations) but not cause, because people who choose a diet often differ in other ways; vegetarians, for example, on average smoke less and exercise more.
Controlled trials, where researchers assign the diets, give stronger evidence of cause but are usually short and small.
5. Explain the biological mechanism behind each claim, naming the nutrient and the body process.
6. Reach a balanced, justified conclusion for a particular group of people.

Example of funding bias: a 1967 review of diet and heart disease, by Harvard scientists in the New England Journal of Medicine, played down sugar and blamed dietary fat. In 2016 it emerged that the Sugar Research Foundation, the sugar industry's trade group, had paid for it without disclosure.
notes.tip: When evaluating a claim from a stimulus, write linked to or associated with, not causes. Check the funder and say what kind of study it was.

notes.h: Vegetarian and vegan diets: what they are and their benefits
notes.b: Some people leave animal foods out of their diet. The different types are defined by exactly which foods they exclude, and each has benefits and risks.
points: A vegetarian diet excludes meat and fish; most vegetarians eat eggs and dairy produce (lacto-ovo vegetarians). A vegan diet excludes all animal products, including eggs, dairy produce and honey. Pescatarians eat fish but not meat.

Vegetarian and vegan diets are usually higher in fibre, fruit and vegetables and lower in saturated fat, so on average blood cholesterol and BMI are lower. Observational studies link them to a lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.
They avoid processed and red meat, which are linked to bowel cancer.

Producing plant food generally uses less land and water and releases less greenhouse gas than producing meat, which makes these diets more sustainable. There is more on this in Metabolic roles and nutritional sources.
Ethical reasons include animal welfare.
notes.tip: Write linked to a lower risk, not prevents. These studies are observational, so they show links, not cause.

notes.h: Vegetarian and vegan diets: risks that need planning
notes.b: Leaving out animal foods removes some useful nutrients. These risks call for planning, not avoidance, because each can be replaced by other foods or supplements.
points: Vitamin B12 occurs naturally only in animal foods, so vegans need fortified foods (with nutrients added) or supplements to prevent anaemia and nerve damage. There is more on this in Vitamins.

Iron from plants is less easily absorbed than iron from meat, so vegans should eat iron-rich plants (beans, lentils, green leafy vegetables and fortified cereals) with vitamin C, which helps absorption.
Vegans must get calcium from fortified plant milks, tofu and green vegetables instead of dairy produce.
Iodine comes mainly from milk and seafood, so vegans may be short of it.
The long-chain omega-3 fatty acids are found mainly in oily fish, so vegans and vegetarians who avoid fish get little of them.
Plant proteins must be combined to supply all the essential amino acids, though this is easily done, e.g. beans with cereal.
Teenagers, pregnant women and young children have the highest needs, so a vegan diet for them needs careful planning.
notes.tip: Keep each risk to the nutrient and why it is short, plus one way to replace it. Do not say vegans cannot get enough protein.

notes.h: Vegetarian and vegan diets: the evidence
notes.b: Evidence about these diets mostly comes from large observational studies. Reading the results carefully means knowing what they can and cannot show.
points: A large UK study of people's diets and health over many years, EPIC-Oxford, found that vegetarians had a lower rate of heart disease but a slightly higher rate of stroke than meat eaters, and that vegans had more bone fractures.
Observational findings like these show links that may have other causes, because people who choose these diets also differ in other ways.
Judgement: a well-planned vegetarian or vegan diet can meet all needs, but it must replace the nutrients that meat, fish and dairy produce supply.
notes.tip: If given a study to evaluate, say what it found, then say it shows a link only. Name EPIC-Oxford and give no percentages, as none are required.

notes.h: High-sugar diets: what counts and the recommendation
notes.b: Not all sugar in food is the same. The recommendation applies only to free sugars, so you need to know exactly which sugars count.
points: Free sugars are sugars added to food and drink, plus the sugars in honey, syrups and fruit juice. The sugar inside whole fruit, vegetables and milk is not counted as free sugar.
The World Health Organization (2015) recommends that free sugars make up less than 10% of daily energy intake, and ideally less than 5%.
notes.tip: Fruit juice counts as free sugar but whole fruit does not. Use the 10% and 5% figures exactly.

notes.b: Eating a lot of free sugar harms health in several ways, but a fair evaluation also gives the case for sugar. The amount and the frequency are what matter.
points: Tooth decay: plaque bacteria on teeth ferment sugar to acid, which damages tooth enamel. There is more on this in Mechanical breakdown.

Excess energy from sugar is stored as fat, causing weight gain and obesity, which raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure and some cancers. Obesity is the main link between sugar and type 2 diabetes.
Sugary foods often supply energy with few other nutrients ('empty' energy) and replace more nutritious foods, and sugary drinks add energy without making a person feel full.
Sugar triggers dopamine release (a brain chemical linked to reward), which can drive overeating. There is more on this in Dopamine and endorphins.

Counter-arguments: glucose is the brain's main fuel, and sugar is a quick energy source, useful for example during long endurance exercise or for a person with diabetes whose blood glucose is too low.
Sugar in whole fruit comes with fibre and vitamins and is not the problem; the risk comes from the amount and how often it is eaten.
Policy link: Ireland introduced a tax on sugar-sweetened drinks in 2018.
Judgement: small amounts of free sugar are harmless; frequent, large amounts harm teeth and raise the risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes.
notes.tip: In an evaluation question, give risks with their biological reasons, one counter-argument and a short judgement. Write that sugar is linked to type 2 diabetes through obesity, not that it causes it.

notes.b: Fat is a necessary nutrient, but the type and the amount matter. Too much saturated fat is the main concern.
points: Saturated fats, found in butter, lard, fatty meat and cheese, raise the type of blood cholesterol (LDL) that is deposited in artery walls, narrowing them (atherosclerosis) and raising the risk of heart attack and stroke.
Artificial trans fats, once common in processed foods, are worse than saturated fats.
Replacing saturated fats with unsaturated oils (olive oil, nuts and oily fish) lowers this risk.

Counter-argument: fat is needed for energy, insulation, cell membranes, essential fatty acids and the absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K, so a very low-fat diet can cause deficiencies. There is more on this in Vitamins.
Fat has about twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate, so fatty food makes weight gain easy.
notes.tip: Separate the types of fat: saturated and trans are the harmful ones, and unsaturated oils are the better choice. A good answer also notes that some fat is essential.

notes.b: People such as body-builders eat extra protein hoping to build muscle. The body does not simply store extra protein as muscle.
points: Extra protein beyond needs is not stored as muscle. Excess amino acids are deaminated (the nitrogen part is removed) and the urea is excreted, and the rest is used for energy or stored as fat. There is more on this in Absorption, transport and storage.
Muscle growth depends on training, with enough protein and energy.
High-protein diets based on processed and red meat bring more saturated fat, and they are often low in fibre.
notes.tip: If asked whether a body-builder needs a very high-protein diet, say that excess is deaminated and used for energy or stored as fat, and that muscle growth needs training.

notes.b: Processed foods have been changed by manufacture, such as being cooked, refined or packaged. Many fast and processed foods have a poor nutrient profile.
points: Many processed and fast foods are high in fat, sugar and salt and low in fibre, vitamins and minerals.
Implications include constipation, a higher risk of bowel cancer, heart disease, type 2 diabetes and obesity, and high salt intake linked to high blood pressure. There is more on salt in Minerals.
Counter-point: some processed foods are useful and nutritious, e.g. frozen vegetables, tinned beans and fortified cereals, so the label, not the word processed, is what matters.
notes.tip: Give both sides. Not all processed food is poor, so name the nutrients in the particular food.

notes.b: Some people cut out dairy produce or gluten. For some this is medically necessary, but for others it is a choice that has costs.
points: Dairy-free and gluten-free diets are necessary for people with milk allergy, lactose intolerance (where lactose-free milk is another option) or coeliac disease.

For other people they bring no proven benefit and need care, since dairy produce is the main calcium and iodine source in many Irish diets, and gluten-free products are often lower in fibre and more expensive.
notes.tip: Say who needs these diets and why, then why they bring no proven benefit for others.

notes.h: Skipping meals and very low-energy diets
notes.b: Some people try to lose weight fast by skipping meals or by eating very little (crash diets). This has several biological drawbacks.
points: Skipping meals and very low-energy (crash) diets run down glycogen stores, leading to tiredness and poor concentration.
The body breaks down muscle protein as well as fat, nutrients are likely to be missed, and weight lost quickly is often regained.
notes.tip: Give the biological effects in your answer: glycogen running down, muscle protein broken down and nutrients missed.

keyTerms.definition: A diet containing all the nutrients, water and dietary fibre in the right amounts and proportions to meet a person's needs.
Any diet that does not meet the body's needs, either undernutrition or overnutrition.
A diet with too little energy or too little of a nutrient, such as iron-deficiency anaemia or rickets.
A diet with too much energy or too much of a nutrient, such as the diets that lead to obesity or too much salt.
The state in which the energy taken in from food equals the energy used, so body mass stays the same.
Mass in kilograms divided by the square of height in metres, used to classify weight for adults.
Plant material, mainly cellulose, that human enzymes cannot digest and that adds bulk to faeces.
Sugars added to food and drink, and the sugars in honey, syrups and fruit juice, but not the sugar inside whole fruit, vegetables and milk.
A fat, found in butter, lard, fatty meat and cheese, that raises LDL cholesterol in the blood.
Artificial fats, once common in processed foods, that raise the risk of heart disease more than saturated fats.
The narrowing of artery walls by deposits of cholesterol, which raises the risk of heart attack and stroke.
A study that records people's diets and health without controlling them, which can show links but not cause.
A study in which conditions are controlled, which gives stronger evidence of cause but is usually short and small.
A diet that excludes all animal products, including eggs, dairy produce and honey.
A vegetarian who eats eggs and dairy produce but not meat or fish.

questions.prompt: What is a balanced diet? Give two reasons why dietary fibre is important.
questions.model: A balanced diet contains all the nutrients, water and dietary fibre in the right amounts and proportions to meet a person's needs, with enough energy but not too much. Dietary fibre adds bulk and absorbs water, so faeces are soft and large, which gives the gut muscles something to push against and keeps peristalsis effective, preventing constipation. A high-fibre diet is also linked to a lower risk of bowel cancer, and fibre feeds the bacteria in the colon that support a healthy gut microbiome.

questions.prompt: Explain why the dietary needs of a 15-year-old girl differ from those of a 70-year-old man.
questions.model: The 15-year-old is growing and going through a growth spurt, so she needs more protein, calcium and vitamin D for bones, and more energy per kilogram of body mass than an adult. Because she menstruates, she loses iron in blood each month and so needs more iron. The 70-year-old's metabolic rate and activity usually fall, so he needs less energy. However, he still needs protein to limit muscle loss, calcium and vitamin D to limit bone loss and osteoporosis, fibre to prevent constipation, and water, because the sense of thirst weakens with age.

questions.prompt: A teenager is considering a vegan diet. Research the biological implications of this choice, giving the benefits and the nutrients she would need to plan for.
questions.model: Benefits: a vegan diet is usually higher in fibre, fruit and vegetables and lower in saturated fat, so blood cholesterol and BMI are on average lower, and observational studies link it to a lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes; avoiding processed and red meat lowers the link to bowel cancer. Nutrients to plan for: vitamin B12, which occurs naturally only in animal foods, so she needs fortified foods or supplements to prevent anaemia and nerve damage; iron, which plants supply in a form less easily absorbed, so she should eat iron-rich plants with vitamin C; calcium from fortified plant milks, tofu and green vegetables; iodine, which comes mainly from milk and seafood; long-chain omega-3 fatty acids, found mainly in oily fish; and protein, which must be combined from plant sources to supply all the essential amino acids. Evidence: the EPIC-Oxford study found that vegans had more bone fractures, and that vegetarians had lower heart disease but slightly higher stroke rates than meat eaters; these are observational links that may have other causes. Judgement: a well-planned vegan diet can meet all her needs, but as a teenager she has high needs and must plan carefully.
